body: Welcome. For about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you move past fine and stressed, and find words for what you actually feel.
This is not therapy and there is no test. It is simply a gentle daily practice of noticing what is happening inside you and giving it a name.
Many of us were never taught words for feelings beyond good, bad, fine and tired. Learning more of them is like adding colours to a small box of crayons.
Notice how often you say fine today. You do not have to change it yet; just count, with curiosity, how many times the word does the heavy lifting.
Feelings often show up in the body before the mind catches up. A tight jaw, a heavy chest or restless legs can all be early messages worth noticing.
No feeling is wrong. Envy, boredom, relief and resentment are all part of being human, and naming them simply helps you understand what is going on.
Pause three times today and ask yourself one quiet question: what am I feeling right now? Any answer, even I am not sure, is a good start.
Stressed is often a bundle of several feelings tied together. Underneath it there may be worry, overwhelm, frustration or a fear of letting someone down.
Place a hand on the part of your body that feels most tense right now. Notice the temperature, the pressure and whether it shifts as you breathe.
Sad, angry, afraid, happy, disgusted and surprised are a useful starting set. Most other feeling words grow out of those broad families.
When you feel bad later today, see whether you can get one step more precise. Is it disappointed, lonely, irritated, anxious or something else?
It is common to feel two things at once, such as proud and sad at a goodbye, or relieved and guilty after cancelling plans. Both can be true.
Feelings are not facts, and they are not commands. You can notice anger without shouting, or fear without running, simply by naming it first.
Before bed, write down one word for how today felt overall. Over the coming weeks, these single words will form a quiet map of your inner life.
Look up a list of feeling words and read it slowly. Notice which ones make you think, ah, that is the one I have been feeling lately.
Some families treated certain feelings as off limits. If anger, sadness or even joy felt risky growing up, it may take time to name it calmly now.
Excitement and nervousness often live in the same place. Find where excitement sits in your body, then nervousness: perhaps both are a flutter in the stomach and a quick pulse.
Try replacing I am fine with one honest word when a trusted person asks how you are. Tired, scattered or content all say much more than fine.
Numbness is a feeling too. If you check in and find nothing, notice the blankness itself, as it can be a sign that you are carrying a lot.
Irritation often rises when a need is going unmet, such as rest, food, quiet or respect. Next time you feel prickly, ask what you might be missing.
Name the weather inside you this morning: foggy, bright, stormy, still. A playful image can unlock a feeling when the exact word will not come.
Pick one moment from yesterday that stayed with you. Replay it gently and ask what you felt then, and whether something else was underneath it.
Anxious and excited, ashamed and embarrassed, lonely and alone: small differences between words can change how you respond to yourself.
Shame says I am bad, while guilt says I did something bad. Telling the two apart can soften the way you speak to yourself after a mistake.
Today, check your shoulders when you read an email from someone difficult. The body often names the feeling before the mind does.
Choose three new feeling words this week, such as wistful, uneasy or tender, and see if any of them fit a moment in your day.
Saying I feel hurt lands very differently from saying you always do this. Naming your feeling keeps the conversation open instead of shutting it.
Disappointment is often mistaken for anger. When you feel cross, check whether you were really hoping for something that did not happen.
Set a gentle reminder for midday that simply says feelings check. When it goes off, take one breath and name whatever is there.
Feelings move in waves. Most of them rise, peak and settle within minutes if we let them pass rather than fighting or feeding them.
Catch a moment of pleasant feeling today, however small, such as warmth from a mug or a song you like. Name it: cosy, delighted, soothed.
Boredom can be a useful signal that you need more meaning, challenge or connection. Treat it as information rather than a problem to fix.
When a feeling is hard to name, describe it by shape, size or colour. A grey lump behind the ribs is a perfectly valid starting point.
Tell one trusted person how you are feeling in a single specific word. Then notice how it feels to have said something true out loud.
Overwhelm often means too many feelings at once. Try separating them on paper: one line each for worry, sadness, frustration and anything else.
If a feeling seems too big for its cause, it may be carrying an older feeling with it. Notice that with kindness rather than criticism.
Pay attention to your breathing when you feel calm, then again when you feel tense. The difference can become an early warning signal.
Write a short note to yourself beginning I notice I am feeling. Finish it honestly, without explaining or justifying the feeling.
Gratitude, awe and contentment are quieter feelings that are easy to miss. Look out for one of them today and give it a moment of attention.
Sometimes tired means sleepy and sometimes it means sad, discouraged or lonely. Next time you say you are tired, check which kind it is.
Contempt, scorn and disgust can feel ugly to admit. Naming them privately, without acting on them, is part of understanding yourself honestly.
Calm and flat can look alike from the outside. Notice whether your stillness today feels restful or a little empty, and name which it is.
Practise naming a feeling in the third person, such as there is frustration here. It can create a little space between you and the feeling.
Feelings often carry useful messages. Fear can point to what matters, anger to a boundary crossed and sadness to something you valued.
Watch for a feeling in someone else today, such as a friend's tone or a stranger's face. Guessing quietly helps you name your own feelings too.
Think of a film or song that always moves you. What exactly does it stir up: longing, hope, grief, tenderness? Let the right word arrive slowly.
Ask someone close to you how they are feeling, then listen for the real word underneath their first answer. Give them time to find it.
Jealousy can feel embarrassing to admit. Naming it honestly, even just to yourself, often takes away some of its sting.
Rate the strength of one feeling today from one to ten. Precision about how much you feel is as useful as knowing what you feel.
Try a short body scan before sleep. Move your attention from your feet to your head and name any sensations: warm, buzzing, tight, loose.
Some feelings arrive dressed as thoughts, such as this is pointless. Ask what feeling sits behind the thought; it might be discouragement.
When you notice yourself reaching for your phone, snacks or busyness, pause and ask whether you are trying to avoid a feeling. Name it if you can.
Let a sad feeling simply be there for a minute without fixing it, and see what happens. It often softens more than you would expect.
Happiness has many shades: playful, peaceful, proud, giddy, satisfied. See which shade turns up in your best moment today.
Use the phrase part of me feels when emotions are mixed. Part of me feels excited and part of me feels scared is honest and very human.
Keep a simple feelings log for three days, writing the time and one word. Patterns often appear that are hard to see from the inside.
Hunger, poor sleep and too much caffeine can all colour how you feel. Check the basics before deciding a feeling is about something bigger.
When you feel hurt by someone, try naming it to them calmly with I felt, followed by one clear word. Keep it short and specific.
Your voice changes with your mood. A flat, quick or quiet voice can be a clue to a feeling you have not named yet.
Name a feeling you tend to hide from others. Ask yourself, without pressure, what you fear might happen if someone saw it.
Pride is a feeling many people shy away from. Let yourself name it today when you do something well, even if it is only in your head.
Learn one feeling word from another language that has no neat equivalent in your own. It can be fun to find words for things you already feel.
Notice the feeling just before you say yes to something you do not want to do. Is it dread, obligation, worry about upsetting someone?
Ask yourself what a feeling might need rather than what it means. Sadness may need comfort, fear may need reassurance and tiredness may need rest.
Anger often protects a softer feeling underneath, such as hurt, fear or embarrassment. When anger rises, gently look for what it is guarding.
Before a conversation you are dreading, name how you feel about it. Uneasy, defensive or nervous is a more helpful start than just stressed.
Try drawing your mood today with a few lines or colours. You do not need artistic skill; you are just giving a feeling a place to land.
There is a particular relief when a difficult feeling is finally named. That small loosening is one of the main rewards of this practice.
Share a mixed feeling with someone you trust, for example I am glad and also a bit sad. Notice how they respond to your honesty.
Loneliness can turn up even in a crowd. If you feel it, name it kindly and consider reaching out to one person, even with a short message.
If feelings have felt heavy for a while, it is a strength to talk to someone you trust or a professional. You do not have to carry it alone.
Look back at your one-word notes from the past weeks. Which feelings came up most often, and which ones were rarer than you expected?
Naming a feeling often changes what you do next. A precise word can turn a reaction into a choice.
Spend a minute on a pleasant feeling and stretch it out a little. Savouring joy, ease or warmth is as much a skill as naming discomfort.
Try describing a hard day to someone using three feeling words instead of one. The extra detail helps them understand and support you.
Grief is not only about death. It can follow a move, a change of job, an ending friendship or a version of yourself you left behind.
Hope is a feeling too, quiet and often overlooked. Notice where in your day you felt a small lift of possibility, and name it.
When someone says they are fine, gently ask once more if they would like to say more. Your growing vocabulary can make room for theirs.
Think about how you would have described yesterday a few months ago, and how you might describe it now. Notice the difference in detail.
Vulnerability is often the feeling of saying something true and not knowing how it will land. It can be uncomfortable and still be good.
Pick one feeling as it arrives today and watch it until it fades. Seeing feelings come and go builds trust that you can handle them.
Your feelings are not too much and not too little. They are signals from a living person, and you are learning to read them with care.
Write a short list of the feeling words you now use that you rarely used before. That list is a real, quiet sign of change.
When you need a pause in a heated moment, try saying I need a minute to work out what I am feeling. It is honest and it buys space.
Consider how naming feelings has changed one relationship in your life. Perhaps a conversation went differently, or felt more honest.
Choose a feeling word that describes how you want to feel more often, such as settled, playful or connected. Notice what brings you closer to it.
Today, when someone asks how you are, give an answer that is both kind and true. Fine can stay in your pocket for days when you need it.
You probably recognise your feelings far more quickly than you did at the start. What once took hours to understand may now take only a moment.
Think of naming feelings as a lifelong language you will keep learning. There will always be new shades to discover and new words to try.
Look back over these weeks and name how you feel about the whole journey. Perhaps it is proud, curious, tender or a mixture of all three.
Thank yourself for every time you paused to ask what you were feeling. Those small moments of attention have built a kinder, clearer inner voice.
This is the final note. Keep noticing, keep naming and keep being gentle with whatever you find. Every feeling has a word, and you can find it.
